name: Iceland
summary: Iceland's commercial framework combines a reservation to the IWC moratorium with national licences. Permission to hunt and a year's actual catches are separate questions.

paragraphs.heading: Which rules apply?
paragraphs.text: Iceland rejoined the IWC in 2002 with a reservation to the commercial-whaling moratorium. Within Iceland, the Whaling Act requires a ministry licence and allows regulation of areas, seasons, quantities and equipment. The official statutory compilation inspected for this page is dated October 1, 2026.

paragraphs.heading: Which whales are covered?
paragraphs.text: The government's December 2024 licensing announcement identifies fin and minke whales as the permitted species. It records licences issued to Hvalur hf. for fin whales and to a named minke-whaling vessel. That announcement establishes what was authorised then; it does not establish that either operation caught whales in every subsequent year.

paragraphs.heading: How should the 2026 record be read?
paragraphs.text: Our existing Iceland development note separately attributes the reported end of the 2026 season and proposed reform to their sources. The reported catch and season-duration discrepancy still needs reconciliation with an official catch return. A reported reform plan should not be presented as an enacted prohibition.

name: Norway
summary: Norway conducts commercial minke whaling under its objection to the IWC moratorium and sets national quotas. A quota is a permitted ceiling, not a count of animals caught.

paragraphs.heading: Which rules apply?
paragraphs.text: Norway lodged a formal objection to the IWC commercial-whaling moratorium. Its government describes a national system of annual quotas, vessel monitoring and hunter training for the minke-whale hunt.

paragraphs.heading: What does the 2026 announcement say?
paragraphs.text: The ministry announced a quota of 1,641 minke whales for 2026 on January 30, 2026. It explains that unused quota carried over from earlier years accounts for the increase. This is an authorisation figure, not a 2026 catch return.

paragraphs.heading: What catch is documented here?
paragraphs.text: The same announcement reports 429 whales caught by 10 vessels in 2025. Keeping that year visible prevents the previous season's reported catch from being mistaken for the current season's result.

name: Japan
summary: Japan resumed commercial whaling in 2019 under national management. Its 2026 total allowable catches are documented by species and must be distinguished from actual landings.

paragraphs.heading: Where and under which framework?
paragraphs.text: Japan's withdrawal from the International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling took effect on June 30, 2019. The Fisheries Agency says commercial operations are restricted to Japan's territorial sea and exclusive economic zone. Fin whales were added to the target species in July 2024.

paragraphs.heading: What is authorised for 2026?
paragraphs.text: The Japanese instrument revised September 18, 2026 sets total allowable catches for January 1–December 31, 2026: 56 sei, 153 Bryde’s, 145 minke and 58 fin whales. These are TAC values, not the number actually caught.

paragraphs.heading: Why the document version matters
paragraphs.text: The September amendment moves eight Bryde’s-whale allocations from the coastal category to the factory-ship category, leaving the species TAC unchanged. Older English initial-allocation material should not be substituted for the revised Japanese allocation. Our research-status page retains the unresolved translation and catch-reconciliation questions.

name: Greenland
region: Arctic and North Atlantic · Kingdom of Denmark
framework: IWC subsistence limits and Greenlandic management
summary: Greenland's large-whale hunts are managed within the IWC Aboriginal Subsistence Whaling framework, with distinctions between species and East and West Greenland.

paragraphs.heading: Who is represented?
paragraphs.text: Greenland is a self-governing part of the Kingdom of Denmark and manages its living natural resources. Its account published by the IWC describes large-whale hunting as part of food provision and community life. That account is a source for Greenland's management and community perspective.

paragraphs.heading: Which whales and areas?
paragraphs.text: The IWC framework distinguishes East Greenland minke whales from West Greenland minke, fin, humpback and bowhead whales. A single national number would conceal these separate management areas and species.

paragraphs.heading: Where are the current limits?
paragraphs.text: Consult the IWC's current catch-limits page and Schedule for the applicable quota block, annual strike provisions and carry-over conditions. Those limits are authorisations; reported catches require a separate dated return. This profile links the current rules without reproducing the IWC data table.

name: United States
practice: Aboriginal subsistence and tribal ceremonial frameworks
framework: IWC limits, federal law and community-specific authorisations
species: Eastern North Pacific gray whale · Makah framework in Washington State
summary: Alaska Native bowhead hunting and the Makah Tribe's gray-whale authorisation process are distinct. They involve different communities, stocks and domestic requirements.

paragraphs.heading: Alaska: bowhead whaling
paragraphs.text: The Alaska Eskimo Whaling Commission co-manages the bowhead hunt with federal oversight. Its account on the IWC website describes community sharing, reporting of whales landed and struck but lost, and the relationship between traditional knowledge and scientific research.

paragraphs.heading: Washington State: the Makah framework
paragraphs.text: NOAA granted the Makah Tribe a Marine Mammal Protection Act waiver in June 2024 for a regulated eastern North Pacific gray-whale hunt. A separate hunt permit is required. NOAA's permitting page records a March 2025 application; a waiver or application alone does not establish that a hunt occurred.

paragraphs.heading: Keep stocks and permissions separate
paragraphs.text: The IWC's current catch-limits page treats the Alaska–Chukotka bowhead stock separately from the gray-whale stock associated with Chukotka and Washington State. These shared stock limits must not be presented as an Alaska gray-whale quota or as a U.S.-only catch allowance.

name: St. Vincent & the Grenadines
framework: IWC provisions for the Bequian humpback-whale hunt
summary: The IWC framework concerns the humpback-whale hunt of Bequia. The island, community and species are more informative than treating the whole country as a single generic whaling operation.

paragraphs.heading: Which community and practice?
paragraphs.text: Bequia's community account published by the IWC describes a humpback-whale hunt using open boats and local processing and distribution of whale products. It records the community's own account of the hunt's cultural and food-related role.

paragraphs.heading: Where are the applicable limits?
paragraphs.text: The current IWC catch-limits page contains a multi-year provision for St Vincent and the Grenadines. Read it with the dated Schedule. An older community account's annual shorthand should not replace the current instrument or be mistaken for actual catches.

paragraphs.heading: What does this profile establish?
paragraphs.text: It identifies the community, species and governing source. It does not establish how many whales were taken in 2026, whether the allocation was fully used, or that a hunt occurred every year.
